lead: Above threshold, the gate sets how much charge sits in the channel and the drain voltage drags that charge along. Writing this down gives the two square-law equations, one for the linear region and one for saturation. They give the drain current from the overdrive, the oxide capacitance, the mobility and the width-to-length ratio W/L. Designers use them to size transistors, find on-resistance and transconductance, and estimate delay before running a simulator.
prereq: You need: the region tests from MOS structure; nMOS and pMOS operating regions and VT from Threshold voltage and body effect.

sections.h3: Channel charge and the drift integral

blocks.text: Put the source at 0 V and let x run from 0 at the source to L at the drain. The channel potential V(x) rises from 0 to V<sub>DS</sub>. Above threshold, the inversion charge per unit area is Q<sub>I</sub>(x) = C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)]. Electrons drift with velocity v = µ<sub>n</sub>·dV/dx, where µ<sub>n</sub> is the electron mobility. The current is width × charge × velocity:

I<sub>D</sub> is the same at every x, so multiply by dx and integrate from source (V = 0) to drain (V = V<sub>DS</sub>). The left side gives I<sub>D</sub>·L; the right side gives WµnCox[(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2]. This is the gradual-channel approximation: the field along the channel is assumed much weaker than the field across the oxide.
Write k<sub>n</sub>′ = µnCox, the process transconductance parameter (A/V²), and V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.

The saturation formula is the linear one at V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub>, where the bracket becomes V<sub>ov</sub>²/2. Beyond it the channel is pinched off and the ideal current stays flat. The boundary between the regions is the curve I<sub>D</sub> = ½kn′(W/L)V<sub>DS</sub>², a parabola through the knee of every curve.

Two graphs show the equations. The output characteristics plot ID against VDS for several VGS: each curve rises, bends at VDS = Vov and goes flat, and the flat levels grow as Vov². The transfer characteristic plots ID against VGS at fixed VDS in saturation: zero up to VT, then a parabola. Some syllabi call these the square-law, Shichman-Hodges or SPICE Level 1 equations.

A pMOS obeys the same equations with V<sub>SG</sub>, V<sub>SD</sub> and |V<sub>Tp</sub>| in place of V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and V<sub>T</sub>, and k<sub>p</sub>′ = µpCox. Hole mobility is roughly a third to a half of electron mobility, so a pMOS is made two to three times wider to match an nMOS.
Transconductance gm = ∂ID/∂VGS in saturation: gm = kn′(W/L)Vov = 2ID/Vov, in A/V (siemens). It measures how strongly the gate controls the current, which sets the gain of an amplifier.

On-resistance. Near VDS = 0 the VDS² term is negligible, so ID ≈ kn′(W/L)Vov·VDS and the transistor is a resistor Ron = 1/[kn′(W/L)Vov]. This is the resistance of a closed switch; doubling W halves it, which is why wider drivers are faster.

Design equation. For a required saturation current, W/L = 2ID/(kn′Vov²). To match a pMOS to an nMOS, make (W/L)p = (W/L)n × kn′/kp′. In SPICE Level 1 these numbers appear as KP (kn′), VTO, GAMMA, PHI and LAMBDA; the last is the slope correction in Non-ideal effects.

examples.question: An nMOS has k<sub>n</sub>′ = 100 µA/V², W/L = 20 and V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V, with V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V. Find I<sub>D</sub> and g<sub>m</sub> at V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V, I<sub>D</sub> at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V, and R<sub>on</sub> near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.
steps: V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V ≥ 1.0 V: saturation. I<sub>D</sub> = ½ × 2000 × 1.0² = 1000 µA = 1 mA.
g<sub>m</sub> = 2000 µA/V² × 1.0 V = 2 mA/V (check: 2ID/V<sub>ov</sub> = 2 × 1 mA / 1 V).
examples.answer: I<sub>D</sub> = 1 mA and g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mA/V in saturation; 0.75 mA at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V; R<sub>on</sub> = 500 Ω.

examples.question: In a process with k<sub>n</sub>′ = 100 µA/V² and k<sub>p</sub>′ = 40 µA/V², an nMOS of W/L = 2 is used with V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V and V<sub>Tn</sub> = |V<sub>Tp</sub>| = 0.5 V. Size the pMOS for equal saturation current at full gate drive, and find that current.
steps: Equal current needs k<sub>p</sub>′(W/L)p = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)n, so (W/L)p = 2 × 100/40 = 5.
Full drive: V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>SG</sub> = 1.8 V, so V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.8 − 0.5 = 1.3 V for both.
examples.answer: Make the pMOS W/L = 5 (2.5 times the nMOS); each carries 169 µA.

traps: In saturation the current depends on V<sub>ov</sub>, not V<sub>DS</sub>; putting V<sub>DS</sub> into the square law makes the current keep rising.
The ½ belongs to the saturation formula; dropping it doubles every answer.
Write W/L, not L/W, when rearranging for size.
For a pMOS use V<sub>SG</sub>, V<sub>SD</sub> and |V<sub>Tp</sub>|, all positive, with k<sub>p</sub>′.
R<sub>on</sub> = 1/[k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>] holds only near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, not across the whole linear region.

quiz.q: State the saturation condition and the saturation current of an nMOS.
quiz.a: V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>; I<sub>D</sub> = ½kn′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)².

quiz.q: Why does the ideal current stay flat once V<sub>DS</sub> passes the overdrive?
quiz.a: At V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> the drain-end charge reaches zero and the channel pinches off. Extra drain voltage drops across the short depleted gap, not along the channel, so the channel and its current do not change.

quiz.q: k<sub>n</sub>′ = 50 µA/V², W/L = 10, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.4 V, V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.4 V, V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V. Find I<sub>D</sub>.
quiz.a: V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V; V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>ov</sub>, linear. I<sub>D</sub> = 500 × (1.0 × 0.3 − 0.045) = 127.5 µA.

quiz.q: Same device at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.5 V: find I<sub>D</sub> and g<sub>m</sub>.
quiz.a: Saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = ½ × 500 × 1.0² = 250 µA; g<sub>m</sub> = 500 µA/V² × 1.0 V = 0.5 mA/V.

quiz.q: A transistor must carry a fixed saturation current. If W/L is doubled, what happens to the overdrive and to g<sub>m</sub>?
quiz.a: V<sub>ov</sub>² halves, so V<sub>ov</sub> falls to 1/√2 = 0.707 of its value. g<sub>m</sub> = 2ID/V<sub>ov</sub> rises by √2 = 1.41.

quiz.q: Why is a pMOS of the same W/L weaker than an nMOS, and how is this fixed?
quiz.a: Holes have lower mobility, so k<sub>p</sub>′ = µpCox is two to three times smaller. The pMOS is drawn wider by the ratio k<sub>n</sub>′/k<sub>p</sub>′.

beyond: Simulators use BSIM or EKV models with dozens of parameters; the square law is the hand-analysis first pass. Analog designers now often size transistors with the g<sub>m</sub>/I<sub>D</sub> method, read from simulated curves, because it also works in weak and moderate inversion where the square law fails.

figure.caption: Output characteristics of the first worked example (k<sub>n</sub>′W/L = 2000 µA/V², V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V). Each curve is linear at low V<sub>DS</sub>, bends where it meets the dashed pinch-off parabola and then stays flat; the flat levels 0.25, 1 and 2.25 mA grow as the square of the overdrive. The two dots are the answers of the example.

spec.aria: Drain current against drain-source voltage for gate voltages 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 volts, flat at 0.25, 1 and 2.25 milliamps beyond a dashed pinch-off parabola; dots at 0.75 milliamp for 0.5 volt and 1 milliamp for 2 volts.
